top_items.author: HF Daily Papers
top_items.summary: An arXiv paper (2609.27334) surfaced via HF Daily Papers proposing a just-in-time approach to agentic memory. It critiques dominant write-time curation designs in which a completed task trajectory is irreversibly distilled into a fixed artifact (reflection, workflow, skill, or reasoning strategy) that is later retrieved by similarity. The authors argue this forces systems to decide what is worth remembering before the future query is known, producing query-independent summaries that discard information and must serve many unknown future tasks. The paper instead advocates learning to curate task-adaptive memory at the time the future task is known.
top_items.reasoning: The paper addresses a core architectural weakness in agent memory systems, a topic highly relevant to agent frameworks like Hermes that rely on experience reuse and skill libraries. The technical framing (write-time curation vs. query-time adaptation) is conceptually substantive, but the excerpt provides only the motivation and problem statement without experimental results or implementation details, limiting measurable impact for practitioners right now.
